rubric.why: A second valid example is required by the question.
rubric.description: Names a second valid suspension.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correct example.

Sand mixed with water is a suspension.

rubric.why: Any one of these is commonly classified as a moderately reactive metal.
rubric.description: Names one moderately reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct metal.

rubric.why: A second correct metal completes the response.
rubric.description: Names a second moderately reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correct metal.

rubric.why: Silver has several established uses; any one valid use earns credit.
rubric.description: Gives one application of silver.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct application.

rubric.description: Gives a second application of silver.

items.followUp: State two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Metals commonly react with oxygen to form basic oxides, or react with water or acids to release hydrogen.
rubric.description: States one correct chemical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct reaction or chemical property.

rubric.why: A second chemical property is needed; it should represent a distinct reaction or property.
rubric.description: States a second correct chemical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct correct property.

modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic.
Metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas.

items.followUp: Who discovered the electron? State two of its properties.

rubric.why: The expected textbook attribution is Goldstein, who observed positive canal rays in a discharge tube.
rubric.description: Identifies Goldstein as the discoverer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Goldstein or the relevant canal-ray discovery.

rubric.why: The proton carries one unit of positive charge.
rubric.description: States the proton's charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a positive charge or +1.

rubric.why: The proton has a relative mass of approximately 1 atomic mass unit.
rubric.description: States the proton's approximate mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for approximately 1 amu or its equivalent in kilograms.

rubric.why: Protons are located in the atom's nucleus.
rubric.description: States the proton's location in the atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the nucleus.

modelAnswer: The proton was discovered by Eugen Goldstein through experiments with canal rays.
A proton has a positive charge of +1.
Its relative mass is approximately 1 amu (1.67 x 10^-27 kg).
Protons are present in the nucleus of an atom.

items.followUp: Differentiate between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: A compound has a fixed composition, whereas a mixture can have a variable composition.
rubric.description: Contrasts composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both fixed composition of a compound and variable composition of a mixture.

rubric.why: The constituents of a compound are chemically combined; those of a mixture are physically mixed.
rubric.description: Contrasts how substances are combined.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.description: Contrasts the properties of the constituents and product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this correct contrast.

rubric.why: A compound has a definite chemical formula; a mixture does not have a fixed formula.
rubric.description: Contrasts formula representation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both sides of the contrast.

rubric.why: Compound constituents are separated chemically, while mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: Contrasts methods of separation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct separation-method contrast.

modelAnswer: A compound has a fixed composition, whereas the composition of a mixture can vary.
In a compound, substances are chemically combined; in a mixture, they are physically mixed.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent substances; mixture components retain their properties.
A compound has a definite chemical formula; a mixture has no fixed formula.
The constituents of a compound are separated by chemical methods; those of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.

items.followUp: Define a coordinate covalent bond and explain its formation in the hydronium ion, H3O+.

rubric.why: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond formed by sharing an electron pair.
rubric.description: Defines the bond as a shared electron pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a shared pair in the bond.

rubric.why: In this bond, both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom.
rubric.description: States that one atom supplies both bonding electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the donor-atom feature.

rubric.why: The ammonium ion is a standard example formed when nitrogen donates a lone pair to H+.
rubric.description: Gives and explains the ammonium-ion example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the NH4+ example with nitrogen donating its lone pair to H+.

rubric.why: The hydronium ion is a second standard example, formed when oxygen donates a lone pair to H+.
rubric.description: Gives and explains the hydronium-ion example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the H3O+ example with oxygen donating its lone pair to H+.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom.
In the ammonium ion, NH4+, nitrogen in NH3 donates a lone pair to H+ to form a coordinate covalent bond.
In the hydronium ion, H3O+, oxygen in H2O donates a lone pair to H+ to form a coordinate covalent bond.

items.followUp: Define melting point and explain how intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Boiling point is defined by the temperature at which a liquid's vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point using the vapour-pressure condition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals external pressure.

rubric.why: Different liquids have different boiling points because their nature and volatility differ.
rubric.description: Explains that boiling point depends on the nature of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct statement about the effect of liquid nature or volatility.

rubric.why: More volatile liquids boil at lower temperatures, while less volatile liquids boil at higher temperatures.
rubric.description: Relates volatility to boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct volatility and boiling-point relationship.

rubric.why: Boiling requires molecules to overcome the attractions between them.
rubric.description: Identifies intermolecular forces as affecting boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the intermolecular attractions.

rubric.why: Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome and therefore raise boiling point.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of force strength on boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between force strength and boiling point.

modelAnswer: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure.
The boiling point depends on the nature of the liquid; different liquids have different boiling points.
A volatile liquid has a relatively low boiling point, while a less volatile liquid has a higher boiling point.
When a liquid boils, its molecules must overcome the intermolecular forces of attraction.
Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome and therefore give a higher boiling point; weaker forces give a lower boiling point.
